title: What should I post next, and why?

messages.content: What should I post next, and why?

Post a **tier list**. It's the only move backed by your data, and you have a 56K-view ceiling proving it works.

## The answer: Extracurricular Tier List

Your three tier lists averaged **23,601 views** — nearly **4x your account average of 5,943**. The format is the single most reliable viral trigger you have:

- **56,808 views** (May 18)
- **20,271 views** (June 7)
- **11,729 views** (May 29, with 141 comments — 2.7% engagement)

Nothing else in your account performs like this repeatably. Your College Essay Tips (22 videos!) have a median of **1,995 views**. Study Techniques caps at **2,989**. The tier list is your franchise — and you're under-using it.

**The specific angle to film:** don't just repeat "ECs ranked." Niche it so it's fresh and debate-bait:
- "Extracurriculars ranked for **T20 STEM applicants**"
- "Every EC ranked by **how much admissions officers actually care**"
- "**Summer programs** tier list — which ones are a waste of money"

That last one matters because your Summer Strategy content is dying (1,621 / 1,666 views) — folding it into the tier list format rescues a dead topic.

## Two rules when you post it

**1. Comment-bait the placement.** Your 11.7K tier list got 141 comments by being debatable. End on: *"Comment which tier YOU'D put debate club in — I'll defend my ranking."* Your data is brutal on this: videos with 40+ comments averaged **18,924 views** vs. **2,847** for sub-10-comment videos.

**2. Post it solo.** Do NOT batch it. Your single-post days averaged **8,842 views** vs **4,156** for batch days. Your June 8 tier list only hit 2,993 views — and you posted it alongside 3 other videos that day. You cannibalized your own best format.

## The runner-up (if you want a second slot this week)

A **Common Data Set** video — but only with a controversial, specific hook. Your June 2 CDS video hit **18,283 views and 5.09% engagement** (635 comments — your highest ever). Frame it as exposing a hidden stat: *"The one number Stanford hides in their Common Data Set."* Avoid generic CDS explainers — your June 7 one got **50 views**.

I don't want to post a tier list its getting too repetitive give me a fresh and unique idea. Make it so that it can become a series

Fair. Burning out your one viral format is a real risk. Here's a series your data actually supports — not a guess.

## The series: "Rejected." — real admits decoded

**The format:** Each episode opens on a real applicant who looked like a *guaranteed reject* on paper, then reveals the one unconventional thing that got them in. In medias res, every time.

**Hook template:** *"4.0, 1580, president of 6 clubs — rejected from every T20. This kid had a 3.6 and got into Penn. Here's the difference."*

### Why this works for YOU specifically (not generic advice)

Your single best-performing video of all time is the **grilled cheese essay — 70,110 views**. The account insights nailed why: it won because of *a specific contrarian story with social proof*, not generic advice. This series is that exact mechanism, productized into a repeatable franchise:

- **Curiosity gap + open loop** — "what was the difference?" forces the watch ✓
- **Social proof** — real school name, real stats ✓
- **Negativity wins** (your Nexus framework) — the rejection is the hook, and you're negative to the *mistake*, never the kid ✓
- **Broad → niche down** — "rejected from every T20" catches everyone anxious about admissions, then you niche into the specific lesson ✓

Your myth-busting Application Strategy videos that used this "you don't need X" structure already proved it scales: **21,189** (May 20) and **20,144** (May 21). The pattern holds — when you debunk a misconception with a real story, you hit 15K–70K. When you give flat tactical advice, you get 2K–8K.

### Why it beats the tier list as a series

The tier list is *one* repeated visual. This series has **infinite fresh episodes** because every applicant is a new story — so it never feels repetitive to your audience even though the structure is identical. That's the whole point of a franchise: same skeleton, new flesh every week.

### How to make it a series (8 episodes ready to batch)

Same cold-open structure, swap the story:
1. "3.6 GPA, got into Penn — the essay did it"
2. "No APs, no leadership — accepted to Brown"
3. "Rejected from her state school, got into Cornell"
4. "Worked at Costco instead of doing research — Stanford said yes"
5. "Failed a class sophomore year — Duke admit"
6. "Zero 'prestigious' ECs — full ride to Vanderbilt"
7. "Applied undecided with no spike — UChicago"
8. "1380 SAT, got into a school that rejected 1550s"

Brand it with a consistent visual cue — same on-screen text style, same opening beat ("On paper, this was a reject…"). That's what trains the algorithm and your audience to recognize the franchise.

### Two non-negotiables from your data

- **Comment-bait the end:** *"Comment your stats and the school you're scared of — I'll tell you your real odds."* Videos with 40+ comments averaged **18,924 views** vs **2,847** under 10. This format naturally bait-engages because people *want* their case decoded.
- **Post solo, one per day.** Single posts: **8,842 avg** vs **4,156** batched. Film all 8 in one session, drip one a week.

4.0, 1580, research, president of 3 clubs — rejected from every T20. This kid had a 3.6 and got into Penn. Here's the difference.

Here's the full script, built to your Nexus framework and run against your 10-point checklist. ~52 seconds.

---

## "Rejected." — Episode 1: The Penn Admit

### 🎬 HOOK (0:00–0:06)
> **"4.0. 1580. Research. President of 3 clubs. Rejected from every T20."**
> *(beat)*
> **"This kid had a 3.6 — and got into Penn. Here's the difference."**

**Visual hook (SPG):** Split screen. Left side = a "perfect" applicant resume with green checkmarks, then a red **REJECTED** stamp slams across all of it. Right side = a near-blank page with one handwritten line, then a Penn acceptance letter. The contrast IS the open loop.
**On-screen text (3–7 words):** `4.0 → rejected. 3.6 → Penn.`
*Power word: the slammed "REJECTED" stamp does the work.*

---

### 🔥 INTEREST PEAK (0:06–0:11)
> **"It's not grades. It's not scores. The first kid did everything right — and that was the problem."**

*(This is your "don't fuck this part up" moment — it reframes the whole video and deepens the loop. Why is doing everything right a problem?)*
**Visual:** The resume's green checkmarks flip to gray — identical, forgettable, blending into a wall of 50 identical resumes.

---

### 💡 VALUE (0:11–0:44)

**Golden nugget first (Sandwich):**
> **"The 4.0 kid was a checklist. Every club, every score, every line existed to look impressive. Admissions read 40,000 of those. You blend in."**

> **"The Penn kid had one thing the perfect applicant didn't: a throughline. Everything pointed at the same obsession."**

> **"Her 3.6? She tanked two classes sophomore year. But every activity after that — her job, her blog, her summer — connected to one idea: making transit accessible in her city."**

> **"So her recs talked about it. Her essay lived in it. Her activities proved it. The reader could finish the sentence: *this is the transit girl.*"**

> **"The 4.0 kid? Nobody could finish that sentence. He was just... good at everything. Forgettable."**

**Clear solution (the A→B bridge — no homework left for them):**
> **"So before you add another club, ask one question: if an admissions officer described you in 5 words, what would they say? If you don't know — neither will they."**

**Visual notes for editor:**
- "Wall of 50 identical resumes" graphic when you say *"you blend in"*
- Single red line connecting job → blog → summer → essay when you say *"throughline"* (literally draw the connecting line on screen)
- The "5 words" line: type 5 blank underscores `_ _ _ _ _` on screen, let it sit for processing time

---

### ✅ PROMISE (0:44–0:48)
> **"Build the throughline, and you stop competing with 40,000 perfect kids. You become the only one of you."**

---

### 📣 CTA (0:48–0:52)
> **"Comment your 5 words. I'll tell you if an admissions officer would remember you — or forget you."**

*(Engagement CTA, polarizing, low-effort to answer, naturally bait. This is your reach engine.)*

---

## Checklist audit

| Item | Pass | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Broad | ✅ | "Rejected from every T20" catches every anxious applicant |
| Open loop | ✅ | "Here's the difference" + "that was the problem" = double loop |
| Visual movement | ✅ | Split-screen, slamming stamp, checkmarks flipping gray |
| Clear solution | ✅ | The "5 words" test is the concrete A→B action |
| Viewer depictable | ✅ | They can run the 5-word test on themselves tonight |
| Unique | ⚠️ | "Throughline/spike" exists — your *framing* (checklist vs. finishable sentence) is the fresh angle. Keep that, it's what makes it feel new |
| Under 1 min | ✅ | ~52s |
| Worth $5 | ✅ | Reframes their entire activities list |
| Stakes & curiosity | ✅ | In medias res, "that was the problem" |
| Unskippable hook | ✅ | The 4.0-rejected / 3.6-admit contrast is the most engaging beat |

## Two things before you film

1. **The story has to be real or directionally true.** If "transit girl" is invented, swap in a real former student's throughline — the specificity is what made grilled cheese hit 70K. A fake-feeling story will tank trust (your framework: *don't remove if it removes trust*).
2. **Record per your prep:** dark shirt, camera just above eye level aimed down for authority, captions just below the chin (Zone 3), and the split-screen resume graphic lives in Zone 4. Read line by line, no blinking on the hook.
